heading: PROPHET IDRĪS (عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ)
title: Truth That Raises a Person
scope: 6 CONNECTED STORIES | 10 INTERACTIVE MISSIONS | 10 DAILY ACTIONS
reviewNote: Scholarly, linguistic, and child-safeguarding review required before publication
introduction: This is the second children’s volume of ʿIBRAH Junior, continuing directly from the end of Prophet Adam (AS). The first volume closed with Dadi Jaan giving Imaan and Akhlaq a narrow case containing a pen marked “IDRIS”. That pen now opens a connected story about telling the truth, learning patiently, correcting errors, and serving people without seeking applause.

The Qur’an names Idrīs (AS) a truthful Prophet, says Allah raised him to a high station, and includes him among the patient and righteous (Maryam 19:56–57; Al-Anbiyāʾ 21:85–86). The authentic Miʿrāj report records that Prophet Muhammad ﷺ met Idrīs in the fourth heaven (Sahih al-Bukhari 3207). Those sources are the evidence-bearing core of this volume. They do not supply a long sequence of Idrīs’s daily activities. Accordingly, the ten missions are ten distinct CHILDREN’S APPLICATIONS of these authentic qualities—not ten invented events in the life of Idrīs.

stories.title: The Pen of Truth
stories.subtitle: A mysterious case from Volume 1 becomes the children’s truthfulness notebook.

blocks.text: On Saturday morning, Imaan and Akhlaq found Uncle Sheikh waiting in the lounge with a small travel bag.
"I brought something for both of you," he announced.
Akhlaq sat up immediately. "Remote-control car?"
"Books?" Imaan guessed.
Uncle Sheikh opened the bag and produced two elegant pens.
Akhlaq stared at his. "A pen?"
Imaan tried to sound grateful. "It is... very pen-like."
Uncle Sheikh burst out laughing. "At least you are honest."
He handed them the pens. "These are not special because they are magical. They are special because I want them to remind you of truth, learning, and careful speech."
"Does this have something to do with a prophet?" Imaan asked.
"It does," Uncle Sheikh replied. "Hazrat Idris (A.S.). But his story comes with an important lesson before we even begin."
Akhlaq clicked his pen. "What lesson?"

"We do not know many details about his life from the Qur'an and authentic Sunnah. Over the centuries, people have repeated stories saying that he was the first person to write with a pen, the first to sew clothes, or a great teacher of astronomy. Those may appear in historical writings, but we should not present them to children as certain facts when our strongest sources do not establish them."
Imaan looked impressed. "So the lesson begins with saying, 'I do not know'?"
"Sometimes that is one of the most truthful sentences a knowledgeable person can say."
Uncle Sheikh opened a Qur'an.
"Allah tells us something short but powerful about Idris (A.S.): he was a Siddiq and a Prophet."
"What does Siddiq mean?" Akhlaq asked.
"A person deeply committed to truth - truthful in belief, words, and character. Allah also says that He raised Idris to a high station."
Imaan turned the pen in her fingers. "That sounds more important than being famous for an invention."
"Exactly," Uncle Sheikh said. "We often want a prophet's story to contain a dramatic invention, a giant building, or an exciting object. But Allah chose to highlight Idris's truthfulness and rank."
He continued, "In another place, Allah mentions Idris among those who were patient and righteous."
"Was he really in the fourth heaven?" Akhlaq asked.
"That detail does come through an authentic report," Uncle Sheikh replied. "During the Mi'raj, the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) met Idris (A.S.) in the fourth heaven."
Akhlaq looked at his ordinary black pen again.
"So this pen is not because Idris invented pens?"
"No," Uncle Sheikh said. "It is because I want you to build a habit worthy of the lesson we actually know about him."
He handed each child a small notebook.
On the first page he had written three headings:
WHAT I KNOW
WHAT I THINK
WHAT I NEED TO CHECK
Imaan smiled. "This is a fact-checking notebook."
"It is a truthfulness notebook," Uncle Sheikh corrected gently. "Facts are part of truthfulness. So is admitting uncertainty."
Uncle Sheikh gave them a test.
"Dinosaurs lived with human beings," he said.
Akhlaq immediately wrote under WHAT I NEED TO CHECK.
"Good," Uncle Sheikh said.
"The Qur'an says Idris was a truthful prophet."
Imaan wrote under WHAT I KNOW.
"The exact job Idris did every morning."
Both children wrote WHAT I DO NOT KNOW.
Uncle Sheikh nodded approvingly.
"One reason misinformation spreads," he explained, "is that people enjoy sounding certain. A truthful person does not add confidence to a claim just because the claim sounds interesting."
Before Asr, Imaan wrote her first entry:
I KNOW: Allah praised Idris for truthfulness.
I THINK: A person who loves truth should also love learning.
I NEED TO CHECK: Stories I hear before I repeat them.
Akhlaq wrote:
I KNOW: Idris was a prophet and was raised to a high station.
I THINK: Saying 'I don't know yet' can be a sign of honesty.
I NEED TO CHECK: Whether Uncle Sheikh really promised ice cream.
Uncle Sheikh looked over his shoulder. "That last one is definitely in the authentic family narration."
Everyone laughed.

The pens were still ordinary pens. But now the children valued them for a better reason: they had become reminders that knowledge without honesty can mislead, while truthfulness can raise a person's character.

stories.title: The Rumour in the Science Club
stories.subtitle: A tempting claim travels faster than the evidence.

blocks.text: The next Monday, Akhlaq entered the school science club with a new pen in his pocket and a great deal of confidence in his voice. His teacher had asked everyone to bring an interesting historical discovery to discuss. Akhlaq announced that he had found a marvelous fact that would amaze the entire class.
“Prophet Idrīs invented writing!” he said proudly. “And I have a picture of an ancient pen to prove it.”

Imaan, who had come to help organize the noticeboard, looked up sharply. She remembered Uncle Sheikh’s rule: a picture of an object could not prove who invented it. “Where did you find the information?” she asked.
“A message from a friend. It had lots of stars next to it.”
“Were they the kind of stars astronomers study,” she asked, “or the kind people put around a message to make it look exciting?”
Akhlaq frowned. His friend had added gold star emojis. He had not opened a book, checked a source, or asked a teacher. Still, the message sounded like a beautiful story. He wanted it to be true.

At home, Dadi Jaan brought the narrow case out of the wooden box. Uncle Sheikh joined them and opened Surah Maryam. He read the verse that describes Idrīs as a truthful Prophet. Then he turned to Surah Al-Anbiyāʾ and showed them the verses naming Idrīs among the patient and righteous.
“Do these verses mention an invention?” he asked.
“No,” Imaan replied.
“Then should we say that he certainly invented writing?”
Akhlaq shook his head slowly. “Even if a lot of people repeat it?”
“Even then. An old or popular claim might appear in historical books, but we should tell the reader how certain it is.”
Akhlaq held his pen horizontally, as though it were a bridge he needed to cross. “What if I already told my friends?”
“You can correct it,” Dadi replied. “You need not call your friend dishonest. Perhaps your friend also heard it from someone else.”

At science club the following day, Akhlaq spoke to the teacher before the group began. “Yesterday I shared something as a fact,” he said. “I checked, and I cannot establish it from the Qur’an or authentic Hadith. What the Qur’an clearly tells us is that Idrīs was a truthful Prophet. I should have said, ‘Some historical writings report this, but we need better evidence.’”

The teacher thanked him for making a correction. His friends did not burst into laughter. Several admitted that they too had repeated exciting claims without checking them. Suddenly the exercise changed. Instead of competing to find the most spectacular historical fact, the class began looking for the most reliable source.
That evening, Imaan wrote in the notebook: “A truthful correction is more valuable than an impressive guess.” Akhlaq added beneath it: “Especially when the guess has gold stars around it.”
Dadi closed the case and pointed to a new envelope on the table, this one marked with a small hourglass. “Tomorrow,” she said, “we shall discover how patience helps truth grow into character.”

stories.title: One Page, Many Attempts
stories.subtitle: Patience means returning to the right effort without giving up.

blocks.text: The hourglass envelope carried a simple sentence: GREAT WORK IS OFTEN MADE OF SMALL ATTEMPTS.

Imaan was not pleased with it. Her calligraphy notebook contained three pages of letters that leaned in different directions. She had hoped to write a beautiful title for the school library project, but every attempt looked uneven. Meanwhile, another student had already finished the task.
“I am not talented,” she declared, pushing her notebook away. “Some people can do this immediately.”
Akhlaq looked at the paper. “I could help. I am excellent at explaining why letters have gone wrong.”
“That,” said Dadi Jaan from the doorway, “is a skill best used with great care.”

She opened the Qur’an at Surah Al-Anbiyāʾ. Allah mentions Idrīs together with Ismāʿīl and Dhul-Kifl and says that they were among the patient. Dadi did not tell the children what schoolwork Idrīs might have done, or invent a difficult moment from his life. Instead, she asked what *sabr* should mean for them.
“Does patience mean I sit still and hope my pen becomes clever?” Imaan asked.
“Not at all. You practise, ask for help, and keep your manners when progress is slow.”

Uncle Sheikh suggested a small plan. Imaan would practise for ten minutes, pause, and then try one line again. Akhlaq offered to fetch a ruler, but he was asked not to take over her work. When Imaan made a mistake, she tried a different technique instead of tearing the page.

The next day the letters were still uneven, though slightly more controlled. Imaan felt a flicker of disappointment. Before she could speak, Akhlaq held up her first page beside the latest one. “Look how far your hand has travelled,” he said.
She smiled. “My hand has travelled about six inches.”
“An important journey,” he replied gravely.

By the end of the week, the title was neat enough to display. It was not the most beautiful in the school, and Imaan no longer needed it to be. She had worked honestly and patiently; she was ready to let others enjoy it too.

Then the patience test changed. A younger child accidentally smudged one corner of the paper. Akhlaq braced himself for an angry response. Imaan closed her eyes, took a breath, and asked whether the child was hurt.
“I worked a long time on that,” she admitted gently. “But we can repair the corner together.”
Dadi's hourglass returned to its envelope. “Patience,” she said, “is not only how long you can wait. It is the character you choose while waiting.”
Under the hourglass, Akhlaq found the next clue: A BOOK THAT BORROWED SOMEBODY ELSE'S WORDS.

stories.title: The Library of Borrowed Ideas
stories.subtitle: Truthfulness also means giving other people credit.

blocks.text: A new shelf was being prepared in the school library. Students were invited to make small information cards for a display called “Wonderful Things We Can Learn.” Imaan chose a card about how to find good sources. Akhlaq chose a card about the value of patience, but on the night before the deadline his page was almost empty.

A classmate sent him a beautifully written paragraph. “You can use it,” the message said. Akhlaq copied it into his document and changed a few words. The result looked impressive. He imagined his teacher reading it aloud and praising his excellent writing.
When Imaan saw the page, she was impressed too. “That sounds different from your usual style,” she said.
“I have improved,” Akhlaq replied quickly. But the answer made him uneasy. The borrowed words might be suitable for a display, yet the way he had presented them suggested they were his own.
Uncle Sheikh, listening to the children's conversation, opened the narrow pen case again. “What does it mean to be deeply truthful?” he asked. “Only to avoid speaking an outright lie?”
Akhlaq thought for a moment. “No. You should not give someone a false impression either.”
“Exactly. The Qur'an praises Idrīs with the word *ṣiddīq*. We should not invent a school assignment for Idrīs himself. But we can ask what honesty should look like in our assignments.”

Akhlaq sent a message to his classmate: “Your paragraph helped me. May I quote part of it if I write your name under it?” The classmate agreed. Then Akhlaq replaced the rest of the paragraph with his own words and added a small acknowledgement.
The new page was shorter, but it felt lighter to carry. When the teacher reviewed the display, she pointed out the clear source note and thanked him for making the origin of the quotation visible.
Akhlaq was surprised. He had expected the absence of impressive language to make him look less clever. Instead, the teacher trusted him more.
At home, Dadi asked him to place the pen on the table beside two cards. One said LOOK BRILLIANT. The other said BE TRUSTWORTHY.
He chose the second. “Though,” he added, “I would still like to be brilliant eventually.”
“Then keep learning,” Dadi replied, “and let your learning be honest.”
She handed them the next envelope. Unlike the others, it did not have any shiny symbol. It carried only a small drawing of two hands helping to lift a box.

stories.title: Goodness Without Applause
stories.subtitle: Righteousness becomes visible in how we serve people.

blocks.text: The school was holding a reading afternoon for younger students. Each volunteer had a task: arrange chairs, bring picture books, read aloud, or make a welcoming sign. Akhlaq immediately selected the microphone role. The microphone had a small silver cover that made it look very important.
“Why do you want that job?” Imaan asked.
“Because I have a strong voice,” he said. Then, after a pause, he added, “Also because everyone can see me.”

When the event began, the youngest visitors arrived earlier than expected. Chairs were scattered, and a child was standing alone at the door. The teacher asked Akhlaq to put down the microphone and help with the seating.
He hesitated. The important job was happening somewhere else. If he lifted chairs, nobody might notice. Dadi's fifth envelope seemed to rustle in his pocket: two hands helping to lift a box.

At home the night before, Uncle Sheikh had explained that Surah Al-Anbiyāʾ describes Idrīs among the righteous and mentions Allah's mercy. Righteousness was not merely an attractive word. The children should strive to make their own behavior better through sincere worship and kindness. But no child could earn the sacred standing of a Prophet by collecting badges or volunteering once.

Akhlaq began moving chairs. Imaan helped a younger visitor choose a storybook. Other children joined them, and soon the room was ready. When it was finally time for announcements, the microphone was already being used by another volunteer.
Akhlaq felt disappointed, but he was also glad the afternoon had gone well. A small boy waved at him from the front row. “Thank you for helping me find a seat,” he whispered.
At the end of the event, the teacher thanked the entire group rather than naming a single star helper. On the way home, Akhlaq asked Dadi whether an act counted if no one knew who had done it.
“Allah knows,” she replied. “But remember: it is not for us to measure a child's religious rank. Our responsibility is to make good choices and seek Allah's pleasure.”
Imaan opened her notebook and added a heading: USEFUL EVEN WHEN UNSEEN. Under it she wrote, “Good work can be quiet.”
When they reached home, the last envelope was waiting on the wooden box. It contained a blank card. Across the top were written three words: WHAT WE KNOW.

stories.title: The Exhibition of What We Know
stories.subtitle: A truthful ending leaves room for uncertainty.

blocks.text: The school library exhibition opened on a bright morning. Imaan and Akhlaq had decided that their final display would be called “The Truthfulness Desk.” There would be no invented drawing of a Prophet, no imaginary portrait of ancient events, and no claim that a pen itself possessed special power.
Instead, there were three neat columns: WHAT THE QUR'AN TELLS US, WHAT AN AUTHENTIC HADITH TELLS US, and WHAT WE MUST NOT PRESENT AS CERTAIN.

Imaan placed a card in the first column: “Idrīs (AS) was truthful and a Prophet.” Then she added two more: “Allah raised him to a high station,” and “Allah named him among the patient and righteous.” She wrote the surah and ayah references below each card.
Akhlaq placed another card under the Hadith heading: “In the Miʿrāj account, Prophet Muhammad ﷺ met Idrīs in the fourth heaven.” He wrote Sahih al-Bukhari 3207 underneath.

Their final card mentioned the famous inventions. It read: “Some historical writings associate Idrīs with writing or tailoring. Our cited Qur'an and authentic Hadith evidence does not establish those claims as certain facts.”
A visitor stopped to look. “So you are saying nobody can ever tell any other story about Idrīs?”

“Not exactly,” Imaan explained. “Scholars have recorded additional reports. But we must distinguish what Allah says, what the Prophet ﷺ authentically reported, and what is uncertain. Different sources carry different kinds of authority.”
Another student asked about the fourth heaven. “Does the Qur'an explain exactly how Idrīs was raised?”

Akhlaq looked at Uncle Sheikh, who was standing nearby. Then he answered for himself. “The Qur'an says Allah raised him to a high station, and a sound Hadith tells us that the Prophet ﷺ met him in the fourth heaven. Scholars discuss what the Qur'anic phrase means. We should not pretend to know every detail.”
Uncle Sheikh smiled. “That is a careful answer.”

At the end of the day the library teacher placed the narrow pen case on the desk and asked what it represented. Akhlaq looked at the pen that had once disappointed him because it was not a remote-control car.
“It reminds us to speak truthfully,” he said. “To practise patience. To do good even without praise. And to admit when we need to check something.”
Dadi Jaan listened quietly. The wooden box had once held six envelopes about the beginning of humanity. Now it held a notebook full of questions, corrections, and lessons about good character.
“Are we finished?” Akhlaq asked.
“With this volume,” said Dadi. “But not with learning.” She placed a small folded paper boat beside the case. On its sail was written one name: NŪḤ.
Akhlaq examined the boat. “Does it mean our next story will have water?”
Dadi laughed. “This time, you will have to wait until the story begins.”

Imaan closed the notebook. She had learned something worth carrying into the next world: a good learner does not need to pretend to know everything. Truth, patience and goodness are already a great place to begin.
Closing bridge: The paper boat is an object in the family’s fictional story, introducing the next learning world about Prophet Nūḥ (AS).

missions.title: The Pen and the Promise

discover.text: STORY EPISODE 1 | Maryam 19:56 | SKILL: Being truthful about what we actually know.

discover.label: Discover
discover.text: the situation
Uncle Sheikh asks Akhlaq to explain why the family gave him a pen labelled “IDRIS”. Akhlaq has heard a popular claim that Idrīs invented writing but cannot find it in the Qur’anic verse.
Revelation and child-friendly understanding

discover.label: Evidence
discover.text: Maryam 19:56

Allah describes Idrīs (AS) as ṣiddīq and a Prophet. The term is stronger than merely avoiding an occasional lie: it praises deep truthfulness and integrity. The Qur’an does not say Idrīs invented the pen; that attractive historical claim must not be treated as revelation. Truthful learners are willing to say, “I do not know yet,” without embarrassment.

evidence.arabic: وَاذْكُرْ فِي الْكِتَابِ إِدْرِيسَ ۚ إِنَّهُ كَانَ صِدِّيقًا نَبِيًّا
evidence.meaning: And mention Idrīs in the Book. Indeed, he was a man of truth and a Prophet.

missions.question: Decision moment: what would you do?

choices.text: Announce the invention claim as an unquestionable fact.
Say the pen is a reminder of truthfulness; explain that the invention claim needs checking.
choices.feedback: Careful honesty is not weakness. It protects what the Qur’an actually says and builds trust in the learner.

choices.text: Say nothing because asking questions is embarrassing.

missions.action: Say “I need to check” once today when you are unsure about a claim, and check it with a trusted source or adult.

remember.label: Think about it
remember.text: When is saying “I do not know” a courageous choice?

remember.label: Memory/revision
remember.text: Listen to Maryam 19:56 once, repeat “صِدِّيقًا نَبِيًّا”, then point to its meaning; no automatic memorization requirement for ages 5–6.

missions.title: Truthful Even When Nobody Looks

discover.text: STORY EPISODE 1 | Maryam 19:56 | SKILL: Honesty in private work.

discover.label: Discover
discover.text: the situation
Akhlaq cannot remember one answer in a homework worksheet. The answer book is open nearby, and his teacher expects his own work.
Revelation and child-friendly understanding

discover.label: Evidence
discover.text: Maryam 19:56

The Qur’anic praise of Idrīs as truthful invites children to examine how they speak and behave. Our story does not claim Idrīs took classroom tests. Rather, it uses a familiar school situation to practise consistency: honest answers, honest credits, and a willingness to learn from mistakes.

evidence.arabic: وَاذْكُرْ فِي الْكِتَابِ إِدْرِيسَ ۚ إِنَّهُ كَانَ صِدِّيقًا نَبِيًّا
evidence.meaning: And mention Idrīs in the Book. Indeed, he was a man of truth and a Prophet.

missions.question: Decision moment: what would you do?

choices.text: Copy the answer and claim it was his own.
Skip the whole worksheet in anger.
Try honestly, mark the uncertain answer, and ask for help later.
choices.feedback: Your own honest attempt teaches you more than a perfect-looking borrowed answer.

missions.action: Complete one small piece of schoolwork honestly, clearly identifying any help you received.

remember.label: Think about it
remember.text: Would you still choose honesty if nobody checked the paper?

remember.label: Memory/revision
remember.text: Listen to 19:56 and explain ṣiddīq in your own words; review the previous mission.

missions.title: Before I Share the Exciting News

discover.text: STORY EPISODE 2 | Maryam 19:56 | SKILL: Fact-checking before passing on a claim.

discover.label: Discover
discover.text: the situation
A message says a famous Prophet invented every early tool used by humans. It has bright stars and a “share now” instruction.
Revelation and child-friendly understanding

discover.label: Evidence
discover.text: Maryam 19:56

A believer should value truthful speech. This mission applies the Qur’anic description of Idrīs to the modern habit of forwarding messages. The claim may be interesting, but popularity, graphics, or repetition cannot prove its authenticity. Checking the strength of a source is itself a good habit.

evidence.arabic: وَاذْكُرْ فِي الْكِتَابِ إِدْرِيسَ ۚ إِنَّهُ كَانَ صِدِّيقًا نَبِيًّا
evidence.meaning: And mention Idrīs in the Book. Indeed, he was a man of truth and a Prophet.

missions.question: Decision moment: what would you do?

choices.text: Share immediately so friends are impressed.
Check credible sources and ask an adult before repeating it as fact.
choices.feedback: A short pause now can prevent a large misunderstanding later.

choices.text: Replace the name with another Prophet and share.

missions.action: Before sharing one piece of news today, ask where it came from and verify it if necessary.

remember.label: Think about it
remember.text: Why do exciting stories travel faster than careful explanations?

remember.label: Memory/revision
remember.text: Recall the Qur’anic phrase “صِدِّيقًا نَبِيًّا” without looking, then compare with the displayed text.

missions.title: The Brave Correction

discover.text: STORY EPISODE 2 | Maryam 19:56 | SKILL: Correcting a mistake without humiliating others.

discover.label: Discover
discover.text: the situation
Akhlaq learns that yesterday’s classroom fact was not reliably established. Everyone heard him say it.
Revelation and child-friendly understanding

discover.label: Evidence
discover.text: Maryam 19:56

Truthfulness includes the ability to correct our own claims. We should not invent a conversation from Idrīs’s life to illustrate this. We can, however, show a child how the virtue of truthfulness makes correction dignified. Correction should be calm, specific, and respectful rather than accusing everyone else of ignorance.

evidence.arabic: وَاذْكُرْ فِي الْكِتَابِ إِدْرِيسَ ۚ إِنَّهُ كَانَ صِدِّيقًا نَبِيًّا
evidence.meaning: And mention Idrīs in the Book. Indeed, he was a man of truth and a Prophet.

missions.question: Decision moment: what would you do?

choices.text: Keep repeating it to avoid feeling embarrassed.
Mock the friend who sent it.
Explain that it was uncertain, apologize for presenting it as fact, and show the source.
choices.feedback: A sincere correction earns trust because it shows responsibility.

missions.action: Correct one inaccurate thing you said or wrote, gently and without blaming another person.

remember.label: Think about it
remember.text: What makes a correction easier to accept?

remember.label: Memory/revision
remember.text: Identify which part of Maryam 19:56 is revelation and which is our modern application.

missions.title: A Little Practice Every Day

discover.text: STORY EPISODE 3 | Al-Anbiyāʾ 21:85 | SKILL: Sabr in learning and skill-building.

discover.label: Discover
discover.text: the situation
Imaan has practised a handwriting line many times. It is still imperfect, and another child has finished already.
Revelation and child-friendly understanding

discover.label: Evidence
discover.text: Al-Anbiyāʾ 21:85

Allah mentions Idrīs among those who were patient. The verse does not narrate a particular assignment, hardship, or period of training from his life. Our application uses an ordinary children’s struggle to show that patience can include repeated effort, wise breaks, and respectful requests for help.

evidence.arabic: وَإِسْمَاعِيلَ وَإِدْرِيسَ وَذَا الْكِفْلِ ۖ كُلٌّ مِنَ الصَّابِرِينَ
evidence.meaning: And remember Ismāʿīl, Idrīs, and Dhul-Kifl. All were among the patient.

missions.question: Decision moment: what would you do?

choices.text: Tear the work and call herself hopeless.
Practise a manageable amount, ask for guidance, and try again tomorrow.
choices.feedback: Growth often happens in small steps that are hard to notice at first.

choices.text: Tell the other child they must have cheated.

missions.action: Spend ten calm minutes improving one skill, then take a sensible break.

remember.label: Think about it
remember.text: What would you say to a friend whose progress feels slow?

remember.label: Memory/revision
remember.text: Listen to 21:85 and practise the word “الصَّابِرِينَ” with meaning.

missions.title: Patience with People

discover.text: STORY EPISODE 3 | Al-Anbiyāʾ 21:85 | SKILL: Gentleness when plans are interrupted.

discover.label: Discover
discover.text: the situation
A younger child accidentally smudges Imaan’s carefully made poster before an exhibition.
Revelation and child-friendly understanding

discover.label: Evidence
discover.text: Al-Anbiyāʾ 21:85

Patience is not only enduring physical delay; it can also shape our speech when others make mistakes. The Qur’an praises these Prophets as patient but does not list every situation they encountered. We can practise patience by pausing before speaking, choosing kind words, and seeking help if a situation feels unsafe.

evidence.arabic: وَإِسْمَاعِيلَ وَإِدْرِيسَ وَذَا الْكِفْلِ ۖ كُلٌّ مِنَ الصَّابِرِينَ
evidence.meaning: And remember Ismāʿīl, Idrīs, and Dhul-Kifl. All were among the patient.

missions.question: Decision moment: what would you do?

choices.text: Shout at the child and grab the paper.
Pretend it is fine but make the child feel guilty all day.
Check the child is safe, explain the problem kindly, and repair what can be repaired.
choices.feedback: You can be honest about disappointment and still treat someone gently.

missions.action: When one small frustration occurs today, pause and respond with calm, respectful words.

remember.label: Think about it
remember.text: How is patience different from allowing somebody to hurt you?

remember.label: Memory/revision
remember.text: Recall 21:85’s theme; make a connection between patience and respectful speech.

missions.title: Give Credit Where It Belongs

discover.text: STORY EPISODE 4 | Maryam 19:56 | SKILL: Academic integrity and acknowledging help.

discover.label: Discover
discover.text: the situation
Akhlaq copies a friend’s carefully written paragraph for his school display and is praised for being an excellent writer.
Revelation and child-friendly understanding

discover.label: Evidence
discover.text: Maryam 19:56

The word ṣiddīq invites honest dealings, not merely accurate statements. When we use someone else’s ideas or words, a truthful description of our work acknowledges that help. The modern example is not an event from the life of Idrīs; it teaches how children can imitate the value praised by revelation.

evidence.arabic: وَاذْكُرْ فِي الْكِتَابِ إِدْرِيسَ ۚ إِنَّهُ كَانَ صِدِّيقًا نَبِيًّا
evidence.meaning: And mention Idrīs in the Book. Indeed, he was a man of truth and a Prophet.

missions.question: Decision moment: what would you do?

choices.text: Accept the praise without explaining the source.
Explain whose words he used, ask permission, and rewrite the rest in his own words.
choices.feedback: Trust grows when people know which part of a project is truly yours.

choices.text: Remove his friend’s name to make the text look original.

missions.action: Give proper credit to one person whose idea, help, or words you used today.

remember.label: Think about it
remember.text: Why is giving credit a form of respect?

remember.label: Memory/revision
remember.text: Match ṣiddīq to a real example of honesty in learning.

missions.title: The Helpful Hands Challenge

discover.text: STORY EPISODE 5 | Al-Anbiyāʾ 21:86 | SKILL: Making goodness useful to others.

discover.label: Discover
discover.text: the situation
Akhlaq wants the stage microphone but the reading event needs help arranging chairs and supporting younger children.
Revelation and child-friendly understanding

discover.label: Evidence
discover.text: Al-Anbiyāʾ 21:86

Allah describes Idrīs and the other named servants as among the righteous and mentions admitting them into His mercy. A child cannot claim a particular spiritual rank from completing a game mission. But the Qur’anic word ṣāliḥīn invites the child to ask how everyday actions can be beneficial, sincere, fair, and respectful.

evidence.arabic: وَأَدْخَلْنَاهُمْ فِي رَحْمَتِنَا ۖ إِنَّهُمْ مِنَ الصَّالِحِينَ
evidence.meaning: And We admitted them into Our mercy, for they were among the righteous.

missions.question: Decision moment: what would you do?

choices.text: Refuse all work that is not visible on stage.
Help with the needed task even if nobody applauds it.
choices.feedback: Useful work matters even when it does not receive a microphone or a medal.

choices.text: Make the younger children do the work instead.

missions.action: Do one safe, helpful task for your family or community without asking for a reward.

remember.label: Think about it
remember.text: What does “useful even when unseen” mean to you?

remember.label: Memory/revision
remember.text: Listen to 21:86; identify the word “الصَّالِحِينَ”.

missions.title: Honour without Boasting

discover.text: STORY EPISODE 5 | Maryam 19:57; Al-Anbiyāʾ 21:86; Bukhari 3207 | SKILL: Humility about recognition and religious knowledge.

discover.label: Discover
discover.text: the situation
After helping the class, Akhlaq receives praise and wants to announce that this proves he is better than the other children.
Revelation and child-friendly understanding

discover.label: Evidence
discover.text: Maryam 19:57; Al-Anbiyāʾ 21:86; Bukhari 3207

Allah says He raised Idrīs to a high station. A sound Hadith tells of Muhammad ﷺ meeting Idrīs in the fourth heaven. Scholars discuss the precise interpretation of “raised him to a high station”; the classroom should not claim certainty about the mechanism. Children must not equate this prophetic honour with leaderboard points or popularity at school. Humility means being grateful for opportunities and careful about what one cannot know.

evidence.meaning: And We raised him to a high station.

evidence.arabic: وَأَدْخَلْنَاهُمْ فِي رَحْمَتِنَا ۖ إِنَّهُمْ مِنَ الصَّالِحِينَ
evidence.meaning: And We admitted them into Our mercy, for they were among the righteous.

missions.question: Decision moment: what would you do?

choices.text: Turn the recognition into proof of religious superiority.
Reject kindness from others because praise is always wrong.
Thank Allah, appreciate the team, and keep serving without comparison.
choices.feedback: You can appreciate encouragement without making yourself more important than others.

missions.action: Thank someone who contributed to a success you enjoyed today.

remember.label: Think about it
remember.text: Why can praise be encouraging without measuring our worth?

remember.label: Memory/revision
remember.text: Review 19:57 and the cited Hadith fact; say which source supports each claim.

missions.title: The Truthfulness Exhibition

discover.text: STORY EPISODE 6 | Maryam 19:56–57; Al-Anbiyāʾ 21:85–86; Bukhari 3207 | SKILL: Synthesis: truth, patience, righteous action and evidence literacy.

discover.label: Discover
discover.text: the situation
Imaan and Akhlaq must arrange their exhibition into “Qur’an”, “Authentic Hadith”, and “Not established as certain”.
Revelation and child-friendly understanding

discover.label: Evidence
discover.text: Maryam 19:56–57; Al-Anbiyāʾ 21:85–86; Bukhari 3207

This mission combines the four Qur’anic ayahs and the authentic Miʿrāj report. Idrīs is a truthful Prophet, patient and righteous, honoured by Allah. Beyond these points, many details of his life remain unreported in our strongest sources. The correct achievement for children is not to invent a dramatic biography but to learn reverently, remember accurately, and turn good values into action.

evidence.arabic: وَاذْكُرْ فِي الْكِتَابِ إِدْرِيسَ ۚ إِنَّهُ كَانَ صِدِّيقًا نَبِيًّا
evidence.meaning: And mention Idrīs in the Book. Indeed, he was a man of truth and a Prophet.
And We raised him to a high station.

evidence.arabic: وَإِسْمَاعِيلَ وَإِدْرِيسَ وَذَا الْكِفْلِ ۖ كُلٌّ مِنَ الصَّابِرِينَ
evidence.meaning: And remember Ismāʿīl, Idrīs, and Dhul-Kifl. All were among the patient.

evidence.arabic: وَأَدْخَلْنَاهُمْ فِي رَحْمَتِنَا ۖ إِنَّهُمْ مِنَ الصَّالِحِينَ
evidence.meaning: And We admitted them into Our mercy, for they were among the righteous.

missions.question: Decision moment: what would you do?

choices.text: Put all popular stories under Qur’an because they sound inspiring.
Present the verified evidence clearly and label uncertain historical claims honestly.
choices.feedback: Respect for sacred history means distinguishing what is known, what is reported, and what remains uncertain.

choices.text: Leave out the Qur’an references to make the exhibit shorter.

missions.action: Teach one verified lesson from this volume to a trusted friend or family member and mention its source.

remember.label: Think about it
remember.text: Which habit will you carry from this learning world into the next?

remember.label: Memory/revision
remember.text: Review all four ayahs in reading order; audio-only option and an optional parent-guided recitation check.
PART III — Developer implementation blueprint
A. Product experience and screen flow
01 · World gate The pen case opens after Adam Volume One. Idrīs world preview presents only verified thematic traits.
02 · Story library Select one of six fictional Imaan-and-Akhlaq episodes; narrated audio and text controls.
03 · Evidence panel One approved Qur’anic ayah or Hadith report with source ID, Arabic and meaning; do not visually merge with fiction.
04 · Meaning and vocabulary Explain ṣiddīq, ṣābirīn and ṣāliḥīn at the child’s level.
05 · Decision card Interactive illustrated contemporary dilemma; choices and feedback as authored.
06 · Mini-game Source sort, sequence, kindness planner or credit task; do not turn Prophet into playable figure.
07 · Daily action One optional real-world action. Parent approval optional and non-punitive.
08 · Reflection One question or emoji-supported private response. Do not demand confession.
09 · Revision Review evidence and previous decision after spaced intervals; retries encouraged.
10 · World synthesis Build the truthfulness exhibition; preview Prophet Nūḥ (AS) through the fictional paper-boat clue.

F. Revision and mastery model
After finishing a mission, offer an optional 1-minute recap; schedule gentle reviews around 1, 3, 7 and 21 days where appropriate.

remember.label: Assess three separate things
remember.text: source recognition, lesson understanding and ethical decision reasoning. Do not claim to measure Iman or Taqwa.
Repeat a child’s missed concept with a new helpful explanation; do not reset progress or announce failure publicly.
Actions must not require sensitive personal stories or evidence photos; the app may ask, “Would you like to reflect?” rather than “Prove you did it.”
Allow children to go backward, re-listen, read in Urdu when professionally localized, and access the complete approved Arabic verse from the source panel.
G. Optional seven-day character journey
Day

Do one honest attempt at schoolwork and name any help received.
Practise a difficult skill calmly for ten minutes.
Choose kind words during one small frustration.

Offer one safe helpful action without requesting praise.
Share one verified fact about Idrīs (AS) and cite the verse or Hadith.
H. Safety, scholarly review and release gates
The sacred-source panel for all ten missions must link to exact Qur’an and Hadith references, not generic chapter names.
Mark the Miʿrāj report’s meeting in the fourth heaven as authentic; do not infer a definitive mechanism for Maryam 19:57 from the report alone.
Remove or label uncertain historical stories including Idrīs writing with a pen, first tailoring, astronomy, his era, birth location, exact death and dialogue.
Ensure all source Arabic is checked against an approved licensed muṣḥaf and all recitations reviewed by a qualified teacher.
Check English and Urdu religious terminology with appropriately qualified scholars and language editors.
Confirm correct answers, gentle feedback, age adaptations, accessibility, data minimization and absence of public faith leaderboards.

review.arabic: وَاذْكُرْ فِي الْكِتَابِ إِدْرِيسَ ۚ إِنَّهُ كَانَ صِدِّيقًا نَبِيًّا
review.meaning: And mention Idrīs in the Book. Indeed, he was a man of truth and a Prophet.
And We raised him to a high station.

review.arabic: وَإِسْمَاعِيلَ وَإِدْرِيسَ وَذَا الْكِفْلِ ۖ كُلٌّ مِنَ الصَّابِرِينَ
review.meaning: And remember Ismāʿīl, Idrīs, and Dhul-Kifl. All were among the patient.

review.arabic: وَأَدْخَلْنَاهُمْ فِي رَحْمَتِنَا ۖ إِنَّهُمْ مِنَ الصَّالِحِينَ
review.meaning: And We admitted them into Our mercy, for they were among the righteous.

synthesis.text: The world of Idrīs (AS) reminds us that a brief Qur’anic account can carry profound guidance. Allah praised him as a truthful Prophet, raised him to a high station and mentioned him among the patient and righteous. That is what the sources establish. We honour him best by preserving those truths rather than decorating them with invented biography.

Imaan and Akhlaq's six connected adventures bring the lessons into their world: the temptation to sound impressive, the courage to correct an error, the patience to practise, the honesty to give credit, and the quiet beauty of helping someone else. The child does not win by collecting a spiritual title. The child learns to speak carefully, practise steadily and act kindly.

The last page of the notebook is deliberately left open. Truthfulness is not a badge earned once and placed on a shelf. It is a habit that grows each time we choose honesty over showmanship and learning over careless certainty. And on the table beside the pen case, a paper boat waits for the next world: the story of Prophet Nūḥ (AS), a journey of faith and perseverance.
